extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners representing trademark applicants before the USPTO (particularly those handling foreign-domiciled clients)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and disciplinary expectations for practitioners handling U.S. trademark matters (with emphasis on representation of foreign‑domiciled clients), including signature requirements, practitioner certifications, supervision of non‑practitioner assistance, and imposed sanctions/monitoring obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule — requirement for U.S.-licensed attorney (37 C.F.R. § 2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective August 3, 2019, any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Counsel Rule was intended to (a) increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations; (b) improve the accuracy of trademark submissions to the USPTO; and (c) safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark registry. Practitioners representing foreign-domiciled clients are expected to know and follow this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a),(c),(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures on trademark documents must be signed by a proper person; trademark documents must be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; an electronic signatory must personally enter the signature characters and the combination must be placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signature must be personally entered by the named signatory; signatures entered by someone other than the named signatory or by unauthorized persons violate the rule. The TMEP provides concrete guidance on permitted signature methods (see TMEP §611.01(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of noncompliant signatures — cancellation/invalidity risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If a trademark signature fails to comply because it was entered by someone other than the named signatory or not signed by a proper person, the trademark may be subject to cancellation and resulting registration may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites prior decisions (e.g., In re Dermahose, In re Cowan) and warns that impermissible signing adversely affects the integrity of the federal trademark registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certifications and reasonable inquiry (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1) and (2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner presenting any trademark or patent paper to the USPTO certifies that statements made on personal knowledge are true and that statements made on information and belief are believed to be true; and that, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, (i) the paper is not for an improper purpose, (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument, (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation, and (iv) denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must conduct a reasonable inquiry supporting factual assertions before presenting papers. Violations may jeopardize the probative value of filings, subject false statements to criminal penalties (18 U.S.C. §1001), and expose the practitioner to disciplinary action under §11.18(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of competence (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must be competent in representation, which includes taking reasonable steps to ensure compliance with applicable rules such that filings are made in proper form and supported by reasonable inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of competence violations include not taking reasonable steps to ensure foreign‑domiciled clients' applications were signed in accordance with the USPTO signature rules, presenting trademark documents not signed by the named signatory, failing to timely or accurately notify clients or the USPTO of potential harm, and failing to conduct reasonable inquiry under §11.18.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to act diligently (e.g., not timely notifying clients of signature errors, continuing to work with a filer after discovering improper signatures) constitutes a breach of §11.103 and may be disciplined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep client reasonably informed and explain matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter and explain it to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically requires timely and accurate notification to clients of actual or potential harm to their IP rights resulting from violations of USPTO signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance (37 C.F.R. § 11.503)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner has responsibilities when using non-practitioner assistance and must have adequate measures in place to monitor how non-practitioners handle matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to monitor or implement adequate measures can lead to impermissible filings (e.g., third parties entering the practitioner's signature) and disciplinary liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct involving misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to present documents where the practitioner reasonably should have known that the named signatory had not signed the document and the practitioner knew the USPTO would rely on such documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation of trademark documents (including declarations) under those circumstances meets the §11.804(c) standard for misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of the trademark registration process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional misconduct includes conduct prejudicial to the administration of the trademark registration process, such as failing to take reasonable steps to ensure filings are signed in accordance with USPTO signature rules, presenting unsigned documents, not timely informing the USPTO, and failing to monitor non‑practitioner assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule encompasses actions that undermine the integrity of the registration process and may be treated as aggravating factors in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP guidance on signatures (TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: TMEP states that the person identified as the signatory must personally sign the document (a paralegal/legal assistant/secretary may not sign or enter an attorney's name), a person may not delegate signature authority, and no person may use document signing software to enter or electronically generate someone else's signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP is an agency guidance document practitioners are expected to consult; its signature guidance clarifies the substantive (not technical) nature of the rule and permissible practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of practitioner knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing applicants or registrants before the USPTO are reasonably expected to know the applicable trademark prosecution rules, the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated, and the potential disciplinary consequences when such provisions are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO publishes resources (webpages, TMEP, OED FOIA reading room) that make this information 'ample' and 'readily available.' Lack of awareness is not an adequate defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability for false or fraudulent statements (18 U.S.C. § 1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: False or fraudulent statements presented to the USPTO may be subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware that disciplinary exposure can be accompanied by potential criminal exposure for knowingly false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions available for misconduct (public reprimand, probation, suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary measures include, but are not limited to, public reprimand, probationary periods, and suspension (up to 90 days under certain procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order describes an agreed-upon sanction (public reprimand + six months probation) and a process where, if the OED Director in good faith believes the practitioner failed to comply during probation, an Order to Show Cause may lead to immediate suspension for up to ninety (90) days after procedural steps (15 days to respond, delivery to USPTO Director). The record may be used as aggravating evidence in future proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation monitoring and reporting obligations (terms of imposed sanction)
rubrics_metrics.description: While on probation the practitioner must: cooperate with USPTO inquiries; during probation search the USPTO online trademark search (tmsearch) at least bi‑weekly for applications identifying him/her as attorney of record; promptly inform in writing the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of filings identifying the practitioner as attorney of record that were made without his/her knowledge or consent; and, every three months, submit a written report to the OED Director confirming completion of the bi‑weekly searches and either stating no improper filings were found or providing copies of correspondence sent to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mandatory, recurring compliance obligations for the probationary period (six months in the agreed sanction) and are enforceable; failure to comply can trigger the Order to Show Cause procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cooperate with investigations and allow public dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future USPTO inquiry into improper trademark filings by a named third party and the OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order (including placing it in the OED FOIA Reading Room) and publish a notice in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation is a condition of the sanction; publication of disciplinary orders is routine and may be used in future disciplinary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural waivers and cost allocation in settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: In the agreed settlement, the respondent waives rights to seek reconsideration, review, or otherwise appeal the Final Order; each party bears its own costs incurred to date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement provisions may include waiver of procedural rights and allocation of costs; practitioners should consider these when entering agreements with OED.
